title: Study of a Nude (Étude de nu)

source.label: Wikipedia: Gauguin showed paintings in Impressionist exhibitions held in 1881 and 1882
Fletcher (1921): Gauguin took part in the exhibitions of the Impressionist group in 1880 and 1881

highlight.text: He formed a friendship with Camille Pissarro and visited him on Sundays to paint in his garden. Pissarro introduced him to various other artists.

source.label: Wikipedia: Study of a Nude, oil on canvas

work.text: Mention has already been made of his appearance in 1880 among the Impressionists and of the praise bestowed by Huysmans on one of his pictures for its frank realism. This very nude, however, shows Gauguin massing his shadows, making them heavy and dark, which was the direct contrary to Impressionist practice.

source.author: John Gould Fletcher
source.title: Paul Gauguin, His Life and Art

work.text: The painting depicts a young, nude woman who is arranging a garment. The scene is set in a bedroom with the woman sitting on an unmade bed against a mauve wall that is decorated with a mandolin and a tapestry. … He depicts her body realistically, without idealisation.

moment.text: My Dear Mr. Pissarro; - I accept with pleasure the invitation that you and Mr. Degas were kind enough to extend to me. And naturally in that case I shall abide by all the rules that govern your Societe.
moment.lead: Accepting the Impressionists' invitation to exhibit with them:

moment.text: Gauguin heard of Impressionism and became a devout follower of its theories. He painted pictures in the manner of Camille Pissarro

source.author: John Gould Fletcher
source.title: Paul Gauguin, His Life and Art

matters.text: In 1879 he was earning 30,000 francs a year (about $145,000 in 2019 US dollars) as a stockbroker, and as much again in his dealings in the art market.
Despite the impact the painting had on the Impressionist exhibition, Gauguin was unable to sell it. His wife, Mette, refused to hang the painting in their home.
